nameStory: The "scaup" name comes from their habit of feeding on "scaup" - an old Scottish word for shellfish beds where these ducks love to dive and feast. In North America, they're often called "bluebills" for their distinctive pale blue-gray bills that stand out against their dark heads.
description: The Greater Scaup is a medium-sized diving duck that's built like a little submarine - compact and streamlined for underwater adventures. Males sport glossy dark heads with a greenish-purple sheen, bright white bellies, and pale gray backs, while females are dressed in more subdued browns with white wing patches. These social ducks often gather in massive floating groups called "rafts" that can number in the thousands on open water.

idTips.label: Blue-gray bill
idTips.description: The pale blue-gray bill is broader and more substantial-looking than other diving ducks, with a slight black tip that's visible up close

idTips.label: Male's glossy head
idTips.description: Males have dark heads that shine with green or purple iridescence depending on how the light hits them - like an oil slick shimmer

idTips.label: Bright yellow eyes
idTips.description: Both sexes have striking golden-yellow eyes that seem to glow against their darker head feathers

idTips.label: White wing stripe
idTips.description: In flight, look for a bold white stripe across the wing that extends well into the primary feathers - it's quite noticeable

idTips.label: Female's facial patch
idTips.description: Female birds show a distinctive white patch around the base of their bill that looks like a bright beard against their brown plumage

idTips.label: Diving behavior
idTips.description: Watch them disappear completely underwater for 20-30 seconds at a time, popping up like corks often far from where they went down

habitat: Look for Greater Scaup on large, open bodies of water in New England - especially coastal bays, harbors, and the bigger inland lakes and reservoirs. They prefer deeper waters where they can dive comfortably, often gathering in protected coves and estuaries along the Atlantic coast. During migration, you might spot them on large rivers or any substantial waterway with minimal vegetation.

seasonality.spring: Peak migration time in March and April when large rafts pass through New England waters heading to northern breeding grounds. Males are in their sharpest breeding plumage with the most vibrant head colors.
seasonality.summer: Very few remain in New England during summer as most head far north to breed in Canada and Alaska. Any summer sightings are likely non-breeding birds or stragglers.
seasonality.fall: Return migration begins in October and November, with birds arriving in smaller groups. Both sexes may show duller, more muted plumage as they transition from breeding colors.
seasonality.winter: Most reliable time to find them along the New England coast, where they form large rafts in protected bays and harbors. Birds are in full winter plumage and most easily observed.

funFact: Greater Scaup are such incredible divers they can plunge down 20 feet underwater - that's deeper than a two-story building is tall - and have been recorded going as deep as 33 feet to grab a tasty mollusk from the bottom!
confusionNotes: The tricky part is telling Greater Scaup from their smaller cousin, the Lesser Scaup, but remember "Greater length" - the white wing stripe on Greater Scaup extends much further out on the wing, and their heads have a more rounded, less peaked shape compared to Lesser Scaup's angular head profile.
contextualKnowledge: Don't let the name fool you - "Greater" doesn't mean these are huge ducks, just slightly larger than Lesser Scaup with significant size overlap between the species. In Europe, they're simply called "Scaup" since Lesser Scaup don't occur there, which can cause confusion when reading international field guides.
compareHints: Compared to Ring-necked Ducks, Greater Scaup lack the white ring around the bill and have much more white on their sides and back. Unlike Redheads and Canvasbacks with their distinctive rusty head colors, Greater Scaup males have dark heads with just a subtle iridescent sheen. The key difference from Lesser Scaup is the more extensive white wing stripe and rounder head shape.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its Aythya relatives, Ring-necked Duck is the small, vegetarian cousin with the white bill ring.
Among New England's diving ducks in the same genus, Lesser Scaup are most similar to Greater Scaup but have rounder heads and shorter wing stripes.

Among its Aythya relatives in New England, the Redhead's rounded head shape sets it apart from the wedge-headed Canvasback, while its copper (not dark) head distinguishes it from Ring-necked Ducks and scaups.
Among its diving duck relatives, canvasbacks are much larger than ring-necked ducks and scaup, with that unique sloping head profile no other Aythya duck shares.
Among its Aythya relatives, Tufted Duck is most similar to Ring-necked Duck but has the distinctive drooping head tuft and golden (not yellow) eyes.
Among its Aythya relatives in New England, male Common Pochards most resemble Redheads but have deeper red heads and darker eyes.
